target.title: fix(clawhub): reject calendar-invalid feed timestamps
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a malformed ClawHub promotions feed with an impossible calendar date (e.g. `2026-02-30T00:00:00.000Z`) would be accepted because `Date.parse` silently normalizes it. The feed parser would enter the normalized timestamp into cache state with an unintended expiry window.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuses `parseAbsoluteTimeMs` from `src/cron/parse.ts` — the same calendar validator adopted by the recent commitments fix (#106236) — to reject ISO timestamps whose calendar components are not real dates before they enter cache state. Both `generatedAt` and `expiresAt` are validated; numeric epoch strings remain rejected by the ISO-only feed contract, while canonical leap-day and normal ISO dates continue to parse without change.

## User Impact

Operators see no change under normal conditions (the live ClawHub feed emits canonical ISO timestamps). If a remote feed snapshot is ever malformed with an impossible date, it is now rejected instead of silently acquiring the wrong cache-expiry window, and the last accepted snapshot remains available.

## Evidence

**Before** (`upstream/main` at the PR base): `parseClawHubPromotionsFeed` accepted `generatedAt: "2026-02-30T00:00:00.000Z"` and returned the feed unchanged because `Date.parse` normalized the impossible date.

**Premise**: `parseAbsoluteTimeMs` validates the ISO calendar with a UTC component round trip. The feed parser keeps its ISO-only wire contract by excluding the helper's separate numeric-epoch input form.

**After — exact-head non-test runtime proof** (`40a0390b559bfde3eb8ceea226a1d85c59fb134c`):

I ran a standalone `node --import tsx --input-type=module -` script with an isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`. The script started a real localhost HTTP server, pointed `OPENCLAW_CLAWHUB_URL` at it, and called the production `maybeRefreshPromotionsFeed` without an injected `fetchImpl`. The server first returned valid sequence 4 / ETag `"v4"`, then calendar-invalid sequence 5 / ETag `"v5"`. It was closed before the final cache read, so the final result came from the real SQLite state DB rather than HTTP. This did not load Vitest or set `NODE_ENV=test`.

```text
$ git rev-parse HEAD
40a0390b559bfde3eb8ceea226a1d85c59fb134c

$ OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR="$(mktemp -d /tmp/openclaw-pr106942-proof-XXXXXX)" node --import tsx --input-type=module -
{
  "runtime": { "vitest": null, "nodeEnv": null },
  "transport": {
    "realHttpRequests": 2,
    "requests": [
      { "url": "/api/v1/feeds/promotions", "ifNoneMatch": null },
      { "url": "/api/v1/feeds/promotions", "ifNoneMatch": "\"v4\"" }
    ]
  },
  "seeded": {
    "sequence": 4,
    "etag": "\"v4\"",
    "slugs": ["runtime-proof"]
  },
  "afterInvalid": {
    "sequence": 4,
    "etag": "\"v4\"",
    "slugs": ["runtime-proof"]
  },
  "sqliteReadAfterServerClosed": {
    "sequence": 4,
    "etag": "\"v4\"",
    "slugs": ["runtime-proof"]
  }
}
```

This demonstrates that the invalid response reached the production HTTP → parser → SQLite cache path, was rejected, and did not replace the last accepted snapshot. A subsequent read after the HTTP server was closed still returned sequence 4 / ETag `"v4"` from SQLite.

Focused exact-head checks after rebasing onto current `upstream/main`:

```text
$ git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD
(exit 0)

$ ./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check src/infra/clawhub.ts src/infra/clawhub.promotions.test.ts src/infra/promotions-feed.test.ts src/wizard/clack-prompter.test.ts
All matched files use the correct format.

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/clawhub.promotions.test.ts src/infra/promotions-feed.test.ts src/wizard/clack-prompter.test.ts --reporter=verbose
Test Files  2 passed (2)
Tests       29 passed (29)
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       11 passed (11)
[test] passed 2 Vitest shards

$ .agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode branch --base upstream/main --stream-engine-output
autoreview clean: no accepted/actionable findings reported
overall: patch is correct (0.96)
```

The live ClawHub endpoint was not used to manufacture malformed data; it currently emits canonical timestamps. The malformed response was served by a standalone local HTTP process to the production fetch/parser/cache path with an isolated real SQLite state store.
